New York Post | Greg Joyce: The Yankees cannot afford any more additions to their M*A*S*H unit. Unfortunately, at least for Saturday, there is another. Spencer Jones, who's been outstanding at the plate lately, was out of the starting lineup Saturday with a sore foot. For his part, Jones did not seem worried and attributed the soreness to playing in Arizona Friday after jamming his heel earlier in the week against the Twins. Here's hoping he's right.
Yahoo Sports | Tate Mosher: Headed into what was likely his penultimate regular season start of 2026, Cam Schlittler's incredible campaign has the attention of people all over baseball. Cam's been so sensational that he's earned MVP chatter, an award that pitchers rarely hoist. The last to do it? Future Hall of Famer Clayton Kershaw. Earlier on Saturday, MLB's official X account made sure everyone is tracking the similarities between the latter's 2014 season and Cam's 2026 campaign. Whether Schlittler can take home AL MVP or not, it's been a heck of a ride. And you know you've had a brilliant season when you're getting comped to Peak Kershaw.
MLB | Bryan Hoch: All Cam, all the time. The burgeoning ace has been so spectacular that it has become difficult for those closest to him to express just how good he has been. Through 31 starts, his 1.95 ERA trails only Ron Guidry's 1.71 ERA in 1978. His 21 starts of one run or fewer are the most in franchise history. And in the past 11o years, only three pitchers his age or younger have matched him, including Babe Ruth in 1916.
CBSSports | Mike Axisa: Meanwhile, if you hadn't heard, Aaron Judge is headed back to the IL, this time with a calf injury. In the aftermath of the Captain's injury, Axisa takes a look at a few questions for Judge, and for the Yankees at large. For Judge, if he can return in time for a playoff run, how much has the injury set him back? Will he be able to find his timing at the dish? For the Yankees, if Judge is out or ineffective, where does that leave the offense against southpaws? It sure would be nice if Judge returns in good order and quickly finds his footing.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty ($): Speaking of Judge's calf injury, there's a little bit of clarification on its nature, if not its severity or a timeline. The injury is in Judge's inner, lower calf. That part of the calf is important for "sustained activities such as standing or walking uphill." Judge has previously played through calf injuries. This time, however, it's in a spot that makes doing so more difficult. So here we are, with the best hitter in the world back on the IL as the Yanks approach the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
The Scotch Babe Ruth Reached For When He Wanted A Drink
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Babe Ruth was as legendary for his pitching as he was for his hitting, becoming one of the "First Five" baseball players inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame. Ruth's notoriety extended off the field as well, where he was known for excessive drinking and partying. Those aren't unique interests for professional athletes these days, but Ruth's career spanned from 1914 to 1935 — Prohibition in the United States was in effect from 1920 to 1934. The 18th Amendment was no match for the Bambino, however. In the book "The Big Bam: The Life and Times of Babe Ruth," biographer Leigh Montville wrote, "Beer and Scotch and hot dogs were his nutritional supplement of choice" (via The Washington Post). His Scotch of choice was Dewar's.
In 1992, Ruth's former Yankees teammate Charlie Devens recounted how Ruth downed a whole quart of whisky while traveling by train between Boston and New York (via Los Angeles Times). Although Ruth reportedly started drinking beer as a child, Scotch was his go-to drink throughout much of his life. His daughter Dorothy recalled that he "would drink a highball, smoke a cigar and chew tobacco—all at the same time" in her book, "My Dad, the Babe." In a 2014 interview with CBS News, Ruth's daughter Julia specified that Dewar's was his favorite. Dewar's invented the highball in 1892, and Ruth undoubtedly had history with the brand, seeing as he worked at his father's saloon for a time at the beginning of his baseball career.
Dewar's and Babe Ruth have connections to one another's industries
Dewar's relationship with American sports didn't start or end with Babe Ruth. Sir Thomas Dewar, the son of Dewar's founder, was a huge soccer fan and donated the original trophy for the Lamar Hunt U.S. Open, America's oldest ongoing national soccer competition. The trophy still bears his name — The Dewar Cup. In 2021, Dewar's became the official Scotch of the U.S. Open golf championship. The latter connection feels particularly appropriate for Ruth, who was an avid golfer and outdoorsman in addition to being a prolific baseball player.
While Dewar's was Ruth's favorite Scotch, his name has found its way onto another liquor brand's bottle nearly a century after his playing days. In 2024, Remus Bourbon partnered with Ruth's family to create Babe Ruth Reserve, a limited-edition whiskey that combined three separate bourbon mash bills — a nod to Ruth's No.3 Yankees jersey. Babe Ruth Reserve had an initial release of 10,624 bottles, corresponding to Ruth's plate appearances. A subsequent release of 8,399 bottles in 2025 represented his career at-bats.
Funnily enough, Remus Bourbon is named for George Remus, known as "The King of Bootleggers," for his Prohibition-era sales of illegal liquor. It's a fitting connection to Ruth's legacy. Nearly a century later, the Bambino is still readily associated with the booze-soaked world of Prohibition when, whiskey was still America's drink of choice.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- Cam Schlittler sported a significant bruise on his right hamstring as he moved through the visiting clubhouse at Chase Field on Friday afternoon. It was a souvenir from his most recent start, which ended after the Mets’ Bo Bichette connected on a 111.5 mph comebacker.
That ball dented flesh, but Schlittler’s season has been so charmed, even the hard-hit balls are turning into outs. Bichette’s knock ricocheted to catcher Austin Wells, who tossed on to first base, sealing Schlittler’s six scoreless innings that day.
“It’s fun to watch. It’s fun to play behind,” Cody Bellinger said. “Even in the middle of the game, I was like, ‘This is unbelievable.’ You don’t really get that much.”
And while the league has had ample opportunity to take in Schlittler’s dominance, what impresses most from a distance of 60 feet and six inches?
“Probably the composure on the mound,” Wells said. “I think that’s the most impressive, besides obviously the numbers across the board. It’s just the way he handles every inning, every pitch. He expects the best every time he throws the ball. So it’s super impressive.”
That’s good news for the Yankees, who appear to be lining up Schlittler to start a potential Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“You’ve got an ace at the top that’s pitched like that, that’s a good place to start,” manager Aaron Boone said. “He’s been dominant. I think he’s just continued to get better, year in and year out.”
“The expectation is to make the playoffs, and the expectation is to win a championship,” Schlittler said. “We’re in a good spot if we keep playing the way we’re playing.”
With Schlittler deep into his longest season yet, Wells believes his batterymate is finding new layers of sharpness.
“I think we’ve seen games where he doesn’t have the best command, but he still gets through it,” Wells said. “There’s another layer to that command piece, that makes it effectively a little bit wild sometimes. I think when he continues to improve that, he’s just going to continue to get better.”
Schlittler’s 1.95 ERA is the second-lowest by a Yankee through 31 starts since Ron Guidry’s 1.71 ERA in 1978, when “Louisiana Lightning” won the Cy Young and finished second in the MVP race to Jim Rice of the Red Sox.
It was the 21st time Schlittler has allowed one run or fewer. That’s a franchise record, and over the last 110 years, only three pitchers age 25 or younger have had as many: Blake Snell (2018), Dean Chance (1964) and Babe Ruth (1916).
Yet Boone said he’s not surprised by Schlittler’s performance, saying it has been largely in line with what the Yankees saw after his late-season callup in 2025.
“He had about as dominant a postseason outing as you could against the Red Sox, and he has carried that right into this year,” Boone said. “He’s got great stuff, he’s a tremendous competitor and he has a real good way about him -- an ability to make adjustments start to start, not be overwhelmed by a result start to start, and he’s put it all together for a full season now at this level.”

item.content:encoded:
Baseball Hall of Fame pitcher and legendary New York Yankees starter CC Sabathia has told the story many times: Dave Stewart changed his mindset forever at just 9 years old in his hometown Vallejo, California.
Stewart, a three-time World Series champion and World Series MVP during his time pitching for the Oakland Athletics, made a surprise visit to Sabathia’s Boys and Girls Club when he was just a kid. Stewart shared a message of inspiration, and it’s one that stuck with a fellow African American major league great who just so happened to hoist his own World Series trophy in a town known best for their hardware on the diamond.
It’s hard to become a Yankees legend, and it’s even harder to find your name amongst the rarest of rare in Monument Park, where the likes of Mickey Mantle, Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig reside in immortality. On Sept. 26, Sabathia will have his No. 52 retired forever by one of the most iconic franchises in sports, an honor he can’t wait to finally see come to life after learning the shocking news months prior.
But while Sabathia’s on-field accomplishments are Hall of Fame and Monument Park worthy, his off-the-field contributions to the next generation are just as timeless and important.
That was on full display Monday at Alpine Country Club in New Jersey, where Sabathia held his 6th Annual Golf Classic for his PitCCh In Foundation. With golf being his latest sports passion post-retirement, it’s a day Sabathia looks forward to with his friends while making a community impact that feels as good as hitting a hole-in-one.
"It’s always fun to be able to get out on the golf course and obviously raise money for a good cause," he told FOX Business before teeing off alongside the likes of Victor Cruz, Gary Sheffield, JR Smith, Matt Barnes, Ron Harper, Jimmy Rollins, Ja Rule and the list goes on. "Our foundation, the money goes directly to the kids in the Bronx. Our kids back home in our hometown of Vallejo [California], this is a direct effect of people coming out here to play golf.
"I was just sitting down talking to Adam Jones and talking about being able to play golf, and the last six years, the network I’ve been able to build just around the game of golf. I wish I would’ve been playing longer, but I’m here now and excited."
The event raised more than $450,000 to help PitCCh In continue creating opportunities and resources for young people and their families on both coasts in one unforgettable day.
It’s moments like this that have Sabathia excited for this next chapter of his life. Yes, he will still be impacting the game of baseball, whether that be broadcasting, or working with the Yankees and MLB as a whole.
But his foundation is something he holds near and dear to his heart, as does his wife Amber and their four children. In fact, PitCCh In is a true part of the family in their eyes.
"It’s great to see the foundation thriving in retirement. Sometimes in retirement, foundations go by the wayside, or players get busy and different things happen. But this is kind of our fifth child we’ve always said," he said, smiling. "PitCCh In has been such a huge part of not just our lives, but like we said, kids on both coasts [and] our kids’ lives.
"I was just with Derek [Jeter] and he celebrated his 30 years for Turn 2 [Foundation], and just the impact he’s been able to make on the youth just in general. So many different stories, Jeter’s Leaders [Program] and people, in the last 30 years that he’s been able to impact. Hopefully, PitCCh In can continue to be that vehicle for years to come, too."
PitCCh In has done everything from field renovations to baseball clinics, to providing college scholarships and school supplies as ways to impact the communities the Sabathia family cares about most. They also have a mentorship program where, through educational and athletic activities, the lives of the youth involved are strengthened on levels both physical and emotional.
Sabathia’s baseball legacy will be told forever in the halls in Cooperstown and behind the center field wall at Yankee Stadium come Sept. 26. But his story is one that goes well beyond the baseball player.
It’s also the person he is, and the family he’s surrounded by, that continues to support and impact in a way he felt from the very beginning.
"It was big for me when I was a kid, just having people that took interest in my life," he said. "I just think about me being lucky in the situation I was in, whether it was my Boys and Girls Club – there was a guy named Philmore Graham who ran my Boys and Girls Club and took a huge interest in me. My high school baseball coach, my fifth grade teacher, all these different people who made an impact and why I’m sitting here. I want to hopefully be that for a kid."

item.content:encoded:
PCA began the day with 9.8 Wins Above Replacement (WAR) according to the formula used at FanGraphs, which is also referred to as fWAR. After a huge, four-hit performance, which included his 42nd home run and 37th stolen base in a 7-3 Cubs win over the Braves, PCA climbed over the 10-WAR line, finishing at 10.1. That is blowing away the field and then some. Shohei Ohtani ranks second in the Majors at 6.8 fWAR, and that includes both his batting and pitching value.
The 3.3-WAR gap between Crow-Armstrong and Ohtani equals the gap between Ohtani and the duo of Jake Bauers and Bryce Harper, who are tied for 60th in MLB. If that holds, it would be the first time in 70 years that there was a 3-fWAR gap between the No. 1 and No. 2 players -- since Mickey Mantle (11.5) finished well ahead of Duke Snider (7.5) in 1956. The only other players in the Modern Era (since 1900) to lead by at least 3 fWAR are Rogers Hornsby (1925, '29) and Babe Ruth (1919, '20, '23, '26).
Now, before we go any further, let’s acknowledge two points:
- WAR can go both up and down, so PCA’s might theoretically drop back under 10. (He already did once, after briefly getting to exactly 10.0.)
- There are two major versions of WAR, one at FanGraphs and one at Baseball-Reference (also referred to as bWAR). These systems use somewhat different inputs and calculate WAR differently, so while they generally are in the same ballpark, they don’t line up exactly. In Crow-Armstrong’s case, he still leads the Majors in bWAR, but with “only” 9.3 entering Tuesday, or 1.7 ahead of Phillies pitcher Cristopher Sánchez.
A 10-WAR season by both models is still in play for Crow-Armstrong, if hardly guaranteed, with 11 games remaining. But even reaching that plateau via one of the two systems is quite an accomplishment. For PCA, it comes down to being great across the board. (All numbers via FanGraphs, entering Tuesday.)
- His 157 wRC+ (compared to the park-adjusted league average of 100) ranks second in the Majors among qualifiers, behind only Yordan Alvarez.
- His 6.9 baserunning runs above average, which factors in both his stolen bases and general success on the bases, ranks fifth in MLB.
- Because he plays a difficult, up-the-middle position and excels at it, his defensive value is the best in baseball, edging out Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.
While PCA’s final total will be decided between now and Sept. 27, let’s take a closer look at the company he would be keeping, assuming he maintains his place in the 10-WAR club.
Note: We’re looking at total WAR here, as opposed to just hitting or pitching WAR. Total WAR combines offensive, defensive and pitching value, which affects not just Ohtani, but also pitchers who hit prior to the universal DH or even position players who have made rare pitching appearances.
Players with 10-WAR seasons in the 30-team era (since 1998)
Aaron Judge
2025 (10.0 fWAR), 2024 (11.2 fWAR, 10.9 bWAR), 2022 (11.1 fWAR, 10.8 bWAR)
Judge missed large chunks of 2023 and ‘26 to injury, but he notched 10 WAR via at least one of the two systems in three consecutive full seasons. In each of the three, he posted a wRC+ of over 200, or more than twice the league average.
Bobby Witt Jr.
2024 (10.5 fWAR)
Witt was the epitome of a complete player in 2024. He posted his second straight 30-30 season, led all MLB hitters with a .332 average and 211 hits, had a 170 wRC+, won his first Gold Glove with an AL-best 16 Outs Above Average at shortstop, and finished second in the AL MVP vote.
Mookie Betts
2018 (10.2 fWAR, 10.7 bWAR)
Betts’ 2018 campaign was the peak of a five-year period from 2015-19 in which he averaged 8.1 bWAR per season. He led MLB with a .346 average and .640 slugging percentage, hit 32 homers and had a 185 wRC+ on his way to AL MVP honors with the world champion Red Sox.
Mike Trout
2016 (10.4 bWAR), 2013 (10.1 fWAR), 2012 (10.1 fWAR, 10.5 bWAR)
Peak Trout had many thinking he could end up being the best player of all time, and his three 10 WAR seasons represented the peak of the peak. Those seasons resulted in the 2012 AL Rookie of the Year Award, the 2016 AL MVP and a wRC+ low of 167.
Zack Greinke
2009 (10.4 bWAR)
No pitcher has crossed the 10-WAR threshold since Greinke did so with the Royals in 2009. He pitched to a 2.16 ERA in 33 starts across 229 1/3 innings on his way to his first – and only – career Cy Young Award.
Barry Bonds
2004 (11.9 fWAR, 10.6 bWAR), 2003 (10.2 fWAR), 2002 (12.7 fWAR, 11.7 bWAR), 2001 (12.5 fWAR, 11.8 bWAR)
From 2001-04, a period in which he was named NL MVP each year, Bonds was quite possibly the most feared hitter who ever lived. In ’01, he set the single-season home run record by smashing 73, and from 2002-04, he broke and re-broke the all-time single-season mark for intentional walks -- he set a record with 68 in ’02, then was issued an intentional free pass 61 times in ’03 and an unfathomable 120 times in ’04. Even prior to that historic run, Bonds produced 9-plus WAR four times (1990, ’92, ’93 and ’96).
Alex Rodriguez
2002 (10.0 fWAR), 2000 (10.4 bWAR)
A-Rod had one of the greatest walk years in MLB history in 2000, when he posted a 1.026 OPS with 41 home runs and 132 RBIs for the Mariners just before inking a then-record 10-year, $252 million contract with the Rangers. Two years later, he belted a career-best 57 home runs to go along with an MLB-leading 142 RBIs and 389 total bases for Texas.
Randy Johnson
2002 (10.5 bWAR)
The Hall of Fame left-hander won four consecutive NL Cy Young Awards with the D-backs from 1999 to 2002, averaging 9.5 WAR per season. Johnson was most dominant in the final year of that stretch, going 24-5 with a 2.32 ERA (195 ERA+, or 95% better than league average) and 334 strikeouts in 260 innings.
Sammy Sosa
2001 (10.2 bWAR)
Slammin’ Sammy Sosa won the NL MVP Award behind a 66-home run barrage in 1998. But his best season may have actually occurred three years later. In 2001, Sosa posted a 186 wRC+, or production 86% better than league average, behind 64 home runs and 160 RBIs.
Pedro Martinez
2000 (11.7 bWAR), 1999 (11.6 fWAR)
Martinez was quite good in his first season with the Red Sox in 1998, finishing as the runner-up in AL Cy Young Award voting. But that was just an appetizer for the dominance that followed. Martinez won consecutive Cy Young Awards in 1999 and 2000, each time leading the Majors in ERA and the AL in strikeouts.
Kevin Brown
1998 (10.0 fWAR)
Brown was a workhorse for the Marlins, Padres and Dodgers from 1996-2000, and the ’98 campaign -- his lone season with San Diego -- was his finest over that span. The hard-throwing right-hander finished that season with a 2.38 ERA (2.23 FIP) and 5.2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 257 innings for the NL champions.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Cam Schlittler, De Los Yankees, Se Une A Babe Ruth En El Exclusivo «Club De Los Cuatro» De La MLB

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Cam Schlittler salió el domingo del montículo del Yankee Stadium con dos tipos de atención muy diferentes siguiéndole los pasos. Una vino de una bola rebotada a 111,5 mph que le dio en la parte posterior del tendón de la corva derecho. La otra vino de otra salida como titular que hizo que la rotación de los Yankees de final de temporada pareciera girar cada vez más en torno a este lanzador diestro de 25 años.
Schlittler lanzó seis entradas sin encajar carreras en la victoria por 2-0 de los Yankees sobre los Mets, permitiendo un hit y dos bases por bolas, mientras ponchaba a ocho. Ben Rice abrió el marcador con su 38.º jonrón en la primera entrada, y Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la tercera. Schlittler se llevó la victoria y mejoró su balance a 14-6. El lanzador derecho de los Mets, Christian Scott, se llevó la derrota, quedando con un balance de 4-5, y David Bednar cerró el partido sin permitir carreras y con solo tres hits, sumando su 34.º salvamento, después de que Brent Headrick y Paul Blackburn se encargaran de la séptima y la octava entrada.
La victoria dejó a los Yankees con un balance de 86-63, los mantuvo a cuatro partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana y redujo a uno su «número mágico» para clasificarse para la postemporada al comenzar el lunes. Además, supuso la quinta victoria de los Yankees en seis partidos y les dio la victoria en la serie frente a su rival local. La preocupación más inmediata llegó con el último lanzamiento de Schlittler, cuando un batazo de línea de Bo Bichette rebotó en su pierna y fue a parar a Wells, quien completó la eliminación en primera base.
El lunes por la mañana, los Yankees aún no habían anunciado ningún nuevo diagnóstico ni resultado de pruebas de imagen. Schlittler dijo después del partido que esperaba poder salir en su próxima apertura, mientras que Aaron Boone afirmó que esperaba que el lanzador diestro estuviera bien. Esto era importante porque los Yankees no se están limitando a aprovechar el buen momento de un novato de cara a octubre. Schlittler se ha convertido en su mejor arma para evitar que te marquen carreras, y su última salida ha añadido una dimensión histórica que pocos lanzadores de su edad han alcanzado en el último siglo. Este cambio ha transformado rápidamente la conversación sobre los Yankees de octubre.
Boone ve más allá del premio Cy Young
El domingo, Schlittler también se colocó en cabeza en la clasificación de ERA de las Grandes Ligas. Su ERA bajó a 1,95, con 228 strikeouts y un WHIP de 0,90 en 184 2/3 entradas. Los Yankees señalaron tras el partido que sus 228 strikeouts son el séptimo mejor registro de un lanzador en una temporada en la historia del club.
A Boone le preguntaron por el valor de Schlittler para los Yankees y llevó la conversación más allá de la carrera por el premio Cy Young.
«Creo que “valioso” es una buena palabra. Puede que incluso sea el MVP», dijo Boone. «Ha estado increíble. Ha hecho una temporada impresionante, y esperemos que aún le quede mucho por dar».
Aaron Judge, tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana, tenía una opinión diferente, aunque seguía respaldando a su compañero de equipo como el mejor lanzador de la liga.
«Sin duda está lanzando como un MVP», dijo Judge. «El Premio Cy Young existe por una razón: para premiar al mejor lanzador del béisbol. Él tiene mi voto para el Cy Young».
Dos tercios de la temporada lo dicen todo
Las 21 salidas en las que ha encajado pocos carreras ya son un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees. Su promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de 1,95 es también la segunda marca más baja de un lanzador de los Yankees tras 31 salidas desde que Ron Guidry registrara un ERA de 1,71 en ese mismo momento de su temporada de 1978, en la que ganó el premio Cy Young.
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera o menos en seis salidas consecutivas. Contra los Mets, mantuvo la posibilidad de un partido sin hits hasta que Brett Baty conectó un doble en la quinta entrada y terminó con 94 lanzamientos, 60 de ellos strikes. Su bola rápida volvió a arrollar a una alineación que había anotado 12 carreras el día anterior.
El resultado deja a los Yankees con una pregunta sencilla de cara a octubre. Ya no se trata de si Schlittler debe estar entre los primeros del equipo de lanzadores, sino de hasta qué punto los Yankees podrán contar con él cuando empiece la postemporada. Es el líder de la Liga Americana en entradas lanzadas y ha combinado una gran carga de trabajo con una defensa de élite contra las carreras.
Una marca digna de Ruth en el libro de récords
Schlittler no ha encajado más de una carrera en 21 de sus 31 partidos como titular esta temporada, lo que le sitúa en un grupo de cuatro lanzadores de los últimos 110 años con 25 años o menos.
Dean Chance fue titular en 22 partidos de este tipo con los Angels en 1964. Blake Snell lo fue en 21 con Tampa Bay en 2018. Babe Ruth lo fue en 21 con Boston en 1916. Schlittler ahora está a la altura de los tres.
La conexión con Ruth se remonta a la época en que este zurdo estaba en su mejor momento como lanzador, antes de sus años como bateador estrella de los Yankees. Ruth terminó con un balance de 23-12 y una efectividad de 1,75 en 1916.
Para Schlittler, la hazaña tiene que ver con la constancia. Ocho de sus salidas han sido sin carreras, lo que significa que otras 13 terminaron con exactamente una carrera encajada. Eso hace que el 67,7 % de sus salidas se hayan saldado con una carrera o menos.
La salud se convierte en el siguiente reto de los Yankees
La única interrupción del domingo se produjo con el rebote de Bichette. Schlittler se marchó por su propio pie y se fue directo al vestuario. Con 94 lanzamientos, lo más probable es que su jornada ya hubiera terminado de todas formas.
Schlittler fue quien dio la explicación más clara tras el partido.
«Me encuentro bien», dijo Schlittler. «Van a ser un par de días divertidos intentando recuperarme, pero creo que estamos en buena posición».
Los Yankees empiezan el lunes una serie de tres partidos en Minnesota, con Will Warren como lanzador titular previsto. El siguiente turno de Schlittler sería más adelante esta semana si la rotación sigue según lo previsto. Por ahora, los Yankees tienen un número mágico de uno, un lanzador titular de primer nivel que comparte un lugar excepcional junto a Ruth, y una revisión médica que importa más que el debate sobre los premios.
Schlittler dejó claro qué carrera es la más importante para él.
«La expectativa es llegar a los playoffs, y la expectativa es ganar el campeonato», dijo Schlittler. «Estamos en una buena posición si seguimos jugando como hasta ahora».
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

La pelota rebotó hacia el receptor Austin Wells, quien retiró a Bichette con un tiro a la primera base. Schlittler se fue directamente al clubhouse después de la jugada, aunque con 94 pitcheos, su carga de trabajo probablemente ya estaba completa de todas maneras. Brent Headrick entró el relevo en el séptimo episodio.

De lo contrario, Schlittler los limitó a dos boletos mientras ponchaba a ocho.

item.content:encoded:
The most impressive records set by Babe Ruth during his MLB career were as a hitter.
But it’s worth remembering that Ruth was also an exceptional left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox before showing his slugging prowess and eventually being traded to the New York Yankees.
A cool record book achievement on Sunday by Yankees phenom Cam Schlittler served as a good reminder of that, too.
Schlittler achieved his feat on Sunday by throwing a gem against the crosstown rival Mets.
He went 6.0 innings, allowing just one hit and two walks while striking out eight.
Schlittler did exit the game after six innings following a line drive that hit him in the back of his right leg off the bat of Bo Bichette at 111 miles per hour.
Before that, though, he had joined a cool piece of MLB’s history.
Cam Schlittler’s New MLB History
It feels like every start features a new bit of history for Schlittler, but this one is pretty dang cool.
Schlittler is now the fourth pitcher in the last 110 years of age 25 or younger to allow zero or one run in at least 21 of his starts in a season, according to MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch.
Yes, a bit specific, but the point being that Schlittler often totally shuts the other team down.
The most recent pitcher to do it was Blake Snell with the Tampa Bay Rays in 2018.
Before that, you have to go way back to 1964 when Dean Chance accomplished the feat.
And the first to do it? Babe Ruth in 1916.
Cam Schlittler has allowed no more than one run in 21 of his 31 starts this season. In the last 110 years, only three pitchers age 25 or younger have had more in a season:
Blake Snell (2018)
Dean Chance (1964)
Babe Ruth (1916)
— Bryan Hoch ⚾️ (@BryanHoch) September 13, 2026
That’s just such cool company.
Chance achieved it in the middle of the best season of his MLB career, when he won the Cy Young with the Angels in 1964.
Snell continued to be one of the more dominant pitchers, when healthy, of this era.
And then there’s the Babe.
Babe Ruth Pitching
In his career, Ruth made 163 pitching outings, including 147 stats. He had a 2.28 ERA.
The aforementioned 1916 season was his best.
That year, Ruth went 23-12 with a 1.75 ERA in 40 starts (44 appearances overall). He threw 323.2 innings with a 1.074 WHIP. Ruth struck out 170 hitters that year.
The most amazing stat of that season: Ruth allowed zero home runs. Yes, it was still the Dead Ball Era, but that’s astounding.
Ruth had already started to show his hitting ability a bit by 1916. He hit three home runs that season and had a .741 OPS.
Soon enough, he’d be the most famous athlete on the planet. But even before that, Ruth was already a special pitcher.
